Salor bag (chuval)
Wool, silk; knotted pile, assymetrical knot, open on the right; aternate warps slightly depressed

The Salor and Tekke tribes both wove chuvals in the design of this example. In caes such as this, when design alone does not permit accurate attribution, textile scholars often depend on telltale features of the weves to establish provenance. Salor knots, for example, are different from those of the Tekke. Weave structure tends to be more conservative than the design and more specific to a tribe, workshop, or region. In other words, it is easier for a weaver to copy a foreign design than to adopt an entirely new way of weaving. In traditional Turkmen culture, a girl begins to weave at a very young age. By the time she is mature, her hands are so habituated to the repeated motions she has learned since childhood that her hand sfly across the loom. To retrain them would mean the loss of valuable time.
